title: Featherless AI Pricing: Plans and Costs (2026 Guide)
summary: Featherless AI pricing offers flat monthly plans based on concurrency ceilings and context limits, not token counts. Evaluate if they fit your needs.
body_markdown:
## Calling the Featherless AI API from Activepieces workflows


Calling Featherless AI's OpenAI-style API from an[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) HTTP step lets you automate requests and track usage, but it does nothing to the price you pay.


Since the concurrency ceiling is what decides whether the plan fits, the useful job for a workflow is watching that ceiling, not shaving the bill.


Activepieces runs whichever model you've already settled on, using your own provider key at your own rate, so the model spend stays on your Featherless or per-token bill and never passes through ours; a platform that resells you a model has made that choice and set its price before you open it.


Bring-your-own-key starts on the Plus plan, $20 a month with 10,000 credits, where every AI step is 1 credit, and MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production, so it's proven for production use.


You can reach the same flows from Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client.


### Connect Featherless AI through an HTTP step


Because the API follows the OpenAI request shape, you don't need a dedicated connector. Add a trigger (a schedule works well), then an HTTP request step set to POST.


Point it at the chat completions path on Featherless AI's base URL. Put your API key in an Authorization header, and send a JSON body with the model name and your messages. The response comes back as JSON that later steps can read.


### Two jobs that suit the plan


That makes two small jobs practical, which means you can pursue them individually. One is a scheduled summary, such as a morning digest of a document folder.


The other is a model comparison, where one flow sends the same prompt to several open-weight models and stores the answers side by side.


The second job is the one that fits the plan, since switching between models is what you're paying a flat fee for.


### Reading the example screenshot


In the screenshot below, the same pattern appears in a different context: a two-step flow with a trigger and an HTTP step. It has a POST method, an endpoint URL, an Authorization header, and a run-details panel with the JSON going in and out.


The endpoint there belongs to a payment service's token revocation, not Featherless AI, so take only the structure from it. The Featherless AI version swaps the URL and body, and the run panel is where you'll read what each call returned.


### Unattended runs and your concurrency limit


Once a workflow like this runs unattended, each execution is a request counted against your plan. A loop that fans out across models can reach your concurrency limit faster than a person typing would.


### Log usage to see if you need a bigger plan


Add a final step that writes each run's model name and outcome to a spreadsheet or database table. If the API returns token counts in its response, store those too; if it doesn't, log the request count alone.


Most of all, watch for a failed call or a rate-limit response, because it marks the moment your load met the ceiling.


After a few weeks, read the log for two patterns. Frequent rejections at busy hours mean your peak concurrency is above what the plan allows, and a bigger tier or a per-token API is the fix.


A log with few rejections spread across many different models means the plan suits you, and you can stop checking.
